module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Solitary Numbers


*References:*
- [Solitary number (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solitary_number)
- [Solitary number large clubs (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solitary_number#Large_clubs)
-/

@[expose] public section

open ArithmeticFunction.sigma

namespace SolitaryNumber

/--
Two positive integers $m$ and $n$ are friendly if they have the same abundancy index, that
is $\sigma(m) / m = \sigma(n) / n$, expressed via cross-multiplication to avoid rationals.
-/
def Friendly (m n : ℕ) : Prop := 0 < m ∧ 0 < n ∧ σ 1 m * n = σ 1 n * m

/--
A positive integer $n$ is solitary if every friend of $n$ is equal to $n$, i.e. its
abundancy class is the singleton $\{n\}$.
-/
def IsSolitary (n : ℕ) : Prop := 0 < n ∧ ∀ m, Friendly m n → m = n

/--
**Is 10 a solitary number?**  The smallest positive integer whose solitary status is
currently unresolved is $10$, with abundancy index $\sigma(10) / 10 = 9/5$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem is_ten_solitary : answer(sorry) ↔ IsSolitary 10 := by
  sorry

/--
**Existence of an infinite club.**  A *club* is an abundancy equivalence class, i.e.
the set of all positive integers friendly with a given $n$.  It is unknown whether any club
is infinite.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_club_exists :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ n, 0 < n ∧ {m : ℕ | Friendly m n}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end SolitaryNumber

reformulations.difference: The source defines solitary as 'not part of any friendly pair', i.e. there is no m ≠ n with σ(m)/m = σ(n)/n. The Lean uses a reflexive, cross-multiplied relation `Friendly m n := 0 < m ∧ 0 < n ∧ σ 1 m * n = σ 1 n * m` (so `Friendly n n` holds). It defines `IsSolitary n := 0 < n ∧ ∀ m, Friendly m n → m = n`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For positive m, n, σ(m)·n = σ(n)·m in ℕ iff σ(m)/m = σ(n)/n in ℚ (div_eq_div_iff). The conclusion `m = n` handles the reflexive case, so `IsSolitary n` holds iff n > 0 and no positive m ≠ n has the same abundancy. Proved in Lean: `IsSolitary n ↔ 0 < n ∧ ¬∃ m, m ≠ n ∧ 0 < m ∧ (σ 1 m : ℚ)/m = (σ 1 n : ℚ)/n`. Also proved: `IsSolitary n ↔ {m | Friendly m n} = {n}` for n > 0.

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether there are infinitely large clubs (equivalence classes of mutually friendly positive integers). The Lean states `∃ n, 0 < n ∧ {m : ℕ | Friendly m n}.Infinite`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `Friendly` is symmetric and transitive (proved in Lean) and reflexive on positive integers. So `{m | Friendly m n}` for n > 0 is exactly the club of n, and an infinite club exists iff some such set is infinite. Proved in Lean: the right-hand side is equivalent to `∃ n > 0, {m | 0 < m ∧ (σ 1 m : ℚ)/m = (σ 1 n : ℚ)/n}.Infinite`. Consistency check: infinitely many perfect numbers implies the right-hand side (club of 6), matching the source's remark about perfect numbers.

sources_consulted: https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.1001 (J. Ward, Does Ten Have a Friend?)
review.notes:
No findings. Both theorems match Wikipedia's "Friendly number" article (Solitary_number redirects there). `is_ten_solitary` matches the section "Is 10 a solitary number?" with the right polarity (10 is conjectured solitary). `infinite_club_exists` matches "Large clubs": "It is an open problem whether there are infinitely large clubs". The perfect-number context shows this means an infinite club, not arbitrarily large finite ones.

Lean checks in /workspace/review:
- `Friendly 6 28`, `Friendly 30 140`, `Friendly 10 10`, `¬Friendly 10 20`, `¬Friendly 0 0` by decide.
- Within the ranges searched: the club of 6 is [6, 28, 496] (m < 5000), the club of 30 is [30, 140, 2480, 6200, 40640] (m < 50000, matching Wikipedia), and 10 has no friend below 5000.
- Proved `IsSolitary 1` (the predicate is satisfiable), `¬IsSolitary 6`, `¬IsSolitary 0`.
- Proved symmetry and transitivity of `Friendly`, and equivalence with the ℚ abundancy formulation.

Neither statement can be settled by a Lean quirk: positivity is built into `Friendly`, and there is no division or truncated subtraction.

Status: `research open` for both matches the source. The latest Wikipedia revision (2026-06-28) still says 10's classification is unknown and the infinite-club question is open; the 2026 edits only added partial bounds on friends of 10. MathWorld (updated Sep 2026) agrees.

`answer(sorry)` shows as `True` under the default `google.answer` mode; that is repository-wide machinery, not a defect of this file. OEIS pages were behind a Cloudflare challenge and the arXiv API returned 429; neither was needed.

The checkout has pre-existing sandbox changes (`lakefile.toml`, `run/`) that I did not make; the file under review is unchanged.
